4. Types of RNA

mRNA carries the code in codons; tRNA carries one amino acid (as an ester at its 3′ end) and has the anticodon; rRNA plus protein is the ribosome, and rRNA is the catalyst that forms the peptide bond. Full treatment: Section 12.5.

5. Replication

Semiconservative: each daughter helix has one old strand and one new. Helicase unzips, primase lays an RNA primer, DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to a 3′-OH so every new strand grows 5′→3′ (leading strand continuous, lagging strand in Okazaki fragments), and DNA ligase seals the fragments. Details and the DNA extraction lab: Section 12.3.

6. Transcription

RNA polymerase binds the promoter, reads the template strand 3′→5′ and builds mRNA 5′→3′ with U for T; the mRNA matches the coding strand except T → U. Given a template, complement it; given a coding strand, copy it and swap T for U. Introns are spliced out before the mRNA leaves the nucleus. Details and example: Section 12.4.

597184.old:
A year later, Rosa’s A1c is 8.1%, still above her goal, so her nurse practitioner adds a once-daily, long-acting insulin called insulin glargine. Rosa is surprised to learn that her insulin is made by microorganisms. The human insulin gene, or an engineered version of it, is inserted into bacteria or yeast using recombinant DNA, and the cells produce the protein.

Insulin glargine differs from human insulin by three amino acids: a glycine replaces an asparagine at the end of one chain, and two arginines are added to the other. These changes make it release slowly from the injection site, and they were made by changing the DNA, not the protein.

5. Blood glucose control

Insulin (high blood glucose, after a meal) increases glucose uptake and glycogenesis. Glucagon (low glucose; acts on the liver) and epinephrine (stress and exercise; liver and muscle) trigger glycogenolysis, and the liver also runs gluconeogenesis. In the Cori cycle, lactate from muscle goes to the liver, is rebuilt into glucose, and is sent back. Glycogen (α(1→4) chains, α(1→6) branches) is stored in liver and muscle; once the stores are full, extra glucose becomes body fat. Hormone table, fed–fasting timeline, stress hyperglycemia, and diabetes: Section 13.9.

6. Other sugars enter glycolysis

Digestion delivers glucose, galactose, and fructose. In the liver, galactose becomes glucose-6-phosphate (enters at step 2) and fructose is split into three-carbon pieces (enters at steps 5–6), using the same reaction types you classify in glycolysis. So all common hexoses end up as pyruvate. Enzymes and galactosemia: Section 13.6.

7. Regulation of glycolysis

Three enzymes, all at irreversible kinase steps. Hexokinase (step 1) is inhibited by its product glucose-6-phosphate. Phosphofructokinase (step 3), the main control point, is under allosteric control: inhibited by ATP, activated by ADP or AMP. Pyruvate kinase (step 10) is inhibited by ATP or acetyl CoA. Energy-rich cell: glycolysis slows; energy-poor cell: it speeds up. Details: Section 13.5; hormonal control: Section 13.9.

8. Pentose phosphate pathway

A second route for glucose-6-phosphate whose products are NADPH (for lipid biosynthesis) and ribose-5-phosphate (for nucleic acids and the coenzymes ATP, GTP, UTP, CoA, NAD+, FAD). Oxidative stage: glucose-6-phosphate (6 C) → ribulose-5-phosphate (5 C) + CO2, dehydrogenases, NADP+ → NADPH. Non-oxidative stage: isomerization to ribose-5-phosphate. When ribose is not needed, the pentose returns to glycolysis as fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. G6PD deficiency: Section 13.6.

9. Gluconeogenesis vs. glycolysis

Gluconeogenesis makes glucose from pyruvate, lactate, glycerol, or some amino acids; it is anabolic, about 90% in the liver, and runs to refill liver glycogen, to finish the Cori cycle, and to keep the glucose-dependent brain supplied when glycogen is gone. Seven glycolysis steps simply reverse; the three kinase steps (1, 3, 10) cannot run backward, because they are too far downhill in the glycolysis direction, so gluconeogenesis goes around them with different enzymes: step 10 is bypassed by pyruvate → oxaloacetate (ATP) → PEP (GTP); steps 3 and 1 by the hydrolases fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase. Net cost 6 ATP equivalents per glucose versus 2 ATP made by glycolysis. Glucagon stimulates it, insulin inhibits it. Details and the Cori cycle: Section 13.8.

10. Glycogenesis and glycogenolysis step by step

Glycogenesis (glucose → glycogen) takes three steps and needs UTP: glucose-6-phosphate → glucose-1-phosphate (phosphoglucomutase, isomerase); glucose-1-phosphate + UTP → UDP-glucose + PPi; glycogen synthase adds the glucose to the chain and releases UDP. Glycogenolysis (glycogen → glucose-6-phosphate) takes two steps and is not the reverse: glycogen phosphorylase removes a glucose unit with free phosphate, no UDP involved, then phosphoglucomutase makes glucose-6-phosphate, which enters glycolysis at step 2 (muscle) or is hydrolyzed to free glucose by glucose-6-phosphatase (liver only). Full tables, branching enzymes, regulation: Section 13.7.

Two weeks after starting insulin, Rosa skips lunch before a 2 p.m. dental appointment. In the chair she becomes shaky, sweaty and confused. The hygienist checks her blood glucose: 62 mg/dL, which is hypoglycemia (below 70 mg/dL). Following the office’s emergency plan, she gives Rosa 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, four glucose tablets, and rechecks in 15 minutes: 104 mg/dL. The appointment continues after Rosa eats a snack.

Later her nurse practitioner reviews how insulin, glucagon and metformin control blood glucose, adjusts her glargine dose, and reminds her not to skip meals.

2. β-Oxidation (in the mitochondria)

Three stages: activation (acyl CoA synthetase, a ligase; ATP → AMP, so 2 ATP-equivalents, once), transport into the matrix by the carnitine shuttle, and the fatty acid spiral. Each repetition is four reactions, the citric acid cycle pattern plus a cleavage: (1) dehydrogenation, C–C → trans C=C, FAD → FADH2, oxidoreductase; (2) hydration to a 2° alcohol at the β carbon, lyase; (3) dehydrogenation, alcohol → ketone, NAD+ → NADH, oxidoreductase; (4) thiolysis by CoA–SH (thiolase, a transferase), releasing acetyl CoA and an acyl CoA two carbons shorter. For n carbons: acetyl CoA = n/2, repetitions = n/2 − 1 (the last cut gives two pieces). ATP = (acetyl CoA × 10) + (NADH × 2.5) + (FADH2 × 1.5) − 2. Stearic acid (18 C): 120 ATP; palmitic (16 C): 106. Fat beats carbohydrate per carbon (and about 2.4× the ATP per gram; 9 vs 4 kcal/g) because its carbons are more reduced. Table, figure, and the slicing tip: Section 15.4.

3. Ketone bodies

When the liver has more acetyl CoA than a citric acid cycle short of oxaloacetate can handle (fasting, low-carb diets, uncontrolled diabetes), ketogenesis makes acetoacetate (condensation of 2 acetyl CoA by thiolase in reverse, condensation with a third to HMG-CoA, then cleavage), β-hydroxybutyrate (hydrogenation of the ketone, NADH → NAD+, oxidoreductase), and acetone (spontaneous decarboxylation; leaves in the breath). Heart, muscle, and after a few days the brain burn them. Ketosis is accumulation the buffers can handle; ketoacidosis lowers blood pH (heavy breathing, dehydration, coma); in DKA insulin does not work and ketogenesis runs unchecked. Table, structures, and the clinical reading: Section 15.5.

4. Amino acid metabolism

Amino acids are not stored; the nitrogen comes off first, because the body cannot oxidize N-containing compounds. Transamination (aminotransferase, a transferase; coenzyme PLP from vitamin B6) moves the amino group to α-ketoglutarate, making glutamate and a new α-keto acid: ALT, alanine → pyruvate; AST, aspartate → oxaloacetate. Oxidative deamination of glutamate (glutamate dehydrogenase, an oxidoreductase, NAD+) releases toxic NH4+ and regenerates α-ketoglutarate. The urea cycle (liver; NH4+ → urea) has an entry step (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, ligase, 2 ATP) and four steps: transfer (ornithine transcarbamoylase) → condensation with aspartate (ligase, ATP) → cleavage to arginine + fumarate (lyase) → hydrolysis to urea + ornithine (arginase, hydrolase); step 1 in the matrix, 2–4 in the cytosol; one N from NH4+, one from aspartate; cost 3 ATP. Carbon skeletons: 20 amino acids give 7 products; glucogenic skeletons reach pyruvate or a cycle intermediate, ketogenic ones reach acetyl CoA or acetoacetyl CoA (only Leucine and Lysine are purely ketogenic). Details, figures, and tables: Sections 15.8, 15.9, and 15.10.

5. Fat mobilization and glycerol

Glucagon and epinephrine activate hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue (covalent modification; insulin does the opposite), releasing fatty acids (on albumin) and glycerol into the blood. Glycerol, the only part of a fat that can become glucose, goes to the liver and becomes DHAP in two steps: phosphorylation of the 1° OH (glycerol kinase, transferase, ATP → ADP) to glycerol 3-phosphate, then oxidation of the 2° alcohol to a ketone (glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, oxidoreductase, NAD+ → NADH). DHAP enters glycolysis or gluconeogenesis; two glycerols make one glucose. Mobilization: Section 15.2; glycerol steps and figure: Section 15.4.

6. Getting fatty acids into the mitochondria

A carboxylic acid is unreactive, so acyl CoA synthetase (ligase) first makes the thioester fatty acyl CoA, splitting ATP to AMP + PPi (2 ATP-equivalents). Acyl CoA cannot cross the inner membrane, so carnitine acyltransferase moves the acyl group onto carnitine, acyl-carnitine crosses, and the acyl group is handed back to a matrix CoA (both transferase reactions). Malonyl CoA blocks the shuttle, so a cell building fat does not burn it. Details and the carnitine clinical note: Section 15.3.

7. Unsaturated fatty acids

An existing C=C means that repetition skips the FAD step and starts at step 2: one fewer FADH2 (1.5 fewer ATP) per double bond; a cis–trans isomerase first converts the natural cis bond to the trans-(2,3) bond hydration needs. Acetyl CoA and repetition counts do not change; oleic acid gives 120 − 1.5 = 118.5 ATP. Section 15.4.

8. Lipogenesis vs. β-oxidation

Lipogenesis (acetyl CoA → palmitic acid, 16 C) runs when intake exceeds need, in the cytosol, with NADPH (from the pentose phosphate pathway), on acyl carrier protein (ACP), under insulin. Acetyl CoA reaches the cytosol as citrate; acetyl CoA carboxylase (ligase, biotin, ATP) makes the 3-carbon malonyl CoA, the two-carbon donor that loses CO2 as it adds. Elongation: condensation, hydrogenation (NADPH), dehydration, hydrogenation (NADPH); steps 2–4 are the reverse of β-oxidation steps 3–1. Seven rounds, 7 malonyl CoA, 14 NADPH per palmitate. Full tables: Section 15.6.

9. Protein digestion, nitrogen balance, and essential amino acids

Proteins supply only about 10% of the body’s energy. Digestion is peptide-bond hydrolysis by hydrolases secreted as zymogens: none in the mouth; in the stomach HCl denatures proteins and activates pepsinogen to pepsin; in the small intestine trypsin (cuts after Lys, Arg), chymotrypsin (after Tyr, Trp, Phe, Leu), carboxypeptidase (C-terminus), and aminopeptidase (N-terminus); amino acids are absorbed by active transport. The amino acid pool has three sources: diet, protein turnover, and liver biosynthesis (nonessential only). Nitrogen balance: intake = excretion; negative in starvation, protein-poor diets, wasting illness, burns; positive in growth, pregnancy, convalescence. Essential amino acids (PVT TIM HaLL: Phe, Val, Thr, Trp, Ile, Met, His, Leu, Lys, plus arginine in the lecture’s count) must come from food; the nonessential ones are made from glycolysis and cycle intermediates, three of them (Ala, Asp, Glu) by a single transamination, tyrosine by oxidation of phenylalanine. Sections 15.7 and 15.11.

  • Thinking ketone bodies are always harmful. Mild ketosis is a normal response to fasting; ketoacidosis is the dangerous extreme.
  • Calling thiolase a hydrolase. Step 4 of β-oxidation uses coenzyme A, not water, to break the carbon–carbon bond; it is a transferase. (Pancreatic lipase and arginase, which do use water, are examples of hydrolases in this chapter.)
  • Saying that fatty acids can be made into glucose. Acetyl CoA cannot go back to pyruvate; only the glycerol part of a fat is glucogenic.
  • Mixing up the two aminotransferase reactions. ALT: alanine ↔ pyruvate. AST: aspartate ↔ oxaloacetate. In both, the partner is α-ketoglutarate ↔ glutamate.
  • Thinking both urea nitrogens come from NH4+. One comes from ammonium (via carbamoyl phosphate); the other comes from aspartate.
  • Confusing ketosis with ketoacidosis on a lab report. Ketones alone are not a diagnosis; look at blood glucose, pH, and bicarbonate.
  • Saying glycerol 3-phosphate is reduced to dihydroxyacetone phosphate. A C–OH becoming a C=O is an oxidation; NAD+ is the oxidizing agent and is itself reduced.

  • Counting one too many repetitions for an unsaturated fatty acid. The number of acetyl CoA and the number of repetitions do not change; only the FADH2 count drops, by one per existing double bond.

In the winter, Rosa catches a stomach virus and cannot keep food down for two days. Following the written sick-day plan from her care team, she sips fluids, checks her glucose more often and tests her urine with a ketone strip, which shows moderate ketones. Her nurse practitioner adjusts her medicines until she can eat again. Her daughter notices a fruity smell on her breath.

At a follow-up visit, her lab report includes BUN (blood urea nitrogen) and creatinine to check her kidneys. One year after her deep cleaning, Rosa’s gums bleed much less and her A1c is 7.0%. Studies suggest that treating gum disease can modestly improve blood glucose control, along with the medicines, diet and exercise you have followed through this book.

Diabetes often leaves the mouth dry, and Rosa’s lips are cracked. Before the cleaning, the hygienist coats them with petroleum jelly (petrolatum), a mixture of large alkanes with roughly 25 or more carbon atoms. Rosa jokes that her lips now feel “waterproof.”

That evening, Rosa’s mother, who lives with her, uses home oxygen through a nasal cannula. Her home-health nurse has warned the family never to use petroleum jelly on the mother’s nose or lips and to use a water-based moisturizer instead. In the kitchen, Rosa cooks dinner on a gas stove that burns methane, and a carbon monoxide detector hangs on the wall.

597086.old:
At her diabetes class, a dietitian shows Rosa how to read food labels. She explains that for decades many shortenings and margarines were made by partial hydrogenation: hydrogen gas was added across some of the C=C double bonds of a liquid vegetable oil to make it more solid. The process also turned some of the remaining cis double bonds into trans double bonds. Trans fats raise LDL cholesterol, and the FDA has since removed partially hydrogenated oils from the U.S. food supply, but Rosa still checks the labels on imported snacks.

The dietitian also asks whether anyone at home smokes. Rosa’s husband does. Tobacco smoke contains polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons such as benzo[a]pyrene, and smoking is one of the strongest risk factors for gum disease.

The hygienist measures deep pockets around several of Rosa’s teeth and notices strong bad breath. She explains that the bacteria living in those pockets break down proteins and release volatile sulfur compounds, mainly hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol, CH3SH.

Rosa asks her nurse practitioner why her A1c matters when her glucose meter readings are “usually fine.” The nurse explains that glucose in the blood is always switching between its ring form and a small amount of its open-chain form, which has an aldehyde group. That aldehyde can react with free amino groups on hemoglobin inside red blood cells, attaching the sugar permanently. Red blood cells live about three months, so the percentage of hemoglobin carrying glucose, the A1c, reflects average blood glucose over the past two to three months. 597193.old:
Fate of pyruvate

Two \(\ce{NAD^{+}}\) are reduced to two \(\ce{NADH}\) which need to be oxidized back to \(\ce{NAD^{+}}\) for the process to continue. It happens in different ways depending on whether sufficient oxygen is present, i.e., aerobic condition or aerobic respiration, or if there is no oxygen, i.e., anaerobic condition. The fate of pyruvate also depends on whether the condition is aerobic or anaerobic, as described below.

Aerobic condition

In aerobic conditions, \(\ce{NADH}\) is not oxidized at this stage, it is oxidized to \(\ce{NAD^{+}}\) at the expense of oxygen in mitochondria. The energy released by the oxidation of \(\ce{NADH}\) is used to produce more \(\ce{ATP's}\) in the third stage of catabolism. Pyruvate is also transferred to mitochondria and undergoes oxidation at the cost of \(\ce{NAD^{+}}\) reduced to \(\ce{NADH}\) through a series of reactions catalyzed by a complex of three enzymes and five coenzymes, collectively called the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. The overall reaction is the decarboxylation of pyruvate, i.e., carbon dioxide (\(\ce{CO2}\)) eliminated. The acetyl (\(\ce{CH3-CO-}\)) group is transferred to \(\ce{HS-CoA}\) producing acetyl-\(\ce{CoA}\), as shown in the following reaction.

\(\ce{\underbrace{CH3-\!\!{\overset{\overset{\Huge\enspace\!{\ce{O}}}|\!\!|\enspace}{\ce{C}}}\!\!-\!\!{\overset{\overset{\Huge\enspace\!{\ce{O}}}|\!\!|\enspace}{\ce{C}}}\!\!-O^{-}}_{Pyruvate} + HS-CoA + NAD^{+} ->[\text{Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex}] \underbrace{CH3-\!\!-\!\!{\overset{\overset{\Huge\enspace\!{\ce{O}}}|\!\!|\enspace}{\ce{C}}}\!\!-S-CoA}_{Acetyl\;CoA} + CO2 + NADH + H^{+}}\)

Acetyl-\(\ce{CoA}\) enters into the citric acid cycle, also called the Krebs cycle, in mitochondria, the third stage of catabolism.

The processing of pyruvate under aerobic conditions is also called oxidative decarboxylation or link reaction, which links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle, as explained in the video below.

Two pyruvates are produced per glycolysis of one glucose molecule. The overall reaction of one glucose molecule under aerobic conditions before entry into the citric acid cycle is the following.

\(\ce{\underbrace{C6H12O6}_{Glucose} + 2HS-CoA + 4NAD^{+} + 2ADP + 2Pi -> 2\underbrace{CH3-\!\!-\!\!{\overset{\overset{\Huge\enspace\!{\ce{O}}}|\!\!|\enspace}{\ce{C}}}\!\!-S-CoA}_{Acetyl\;CoA} + 2CO2 + 4NADH + 2ATP + 4H^{+} + 2H2O}\)

There is a net gain of six energetic molecules: \(\ce{2ATP}\) and \(\ce{4NADH}\) from glycolysis and link reaction under aerobic conditions.

Anaerobic condition

During vigorous exercises, as shown in the figure, or strenuous physical work, oxygen depletes in muscles creating anaerobic (oxygen-free) conditions. Under anaerobic conditions, \(\ce{NADH}\) is oxidized to \(\ce{NAD^{+}}\) in the cytosol at the expense of the reduction of pyruvate to lactate, as shown in the reaction below.

\(\ce{\underbrace{CH3-\!\!{\overset{\overset{\Huge\enspace\!{\ce{O}}}|\!\!|\enspace}{\ce{C}}}\!\!-\!\!{\overset{\overset{\Huge\enspace\!{\ce{O}}}|\!\!|\enspace}{\ce{C}}}\!\!-O^{-}}_{Pyruvate} + NADH + H^{+} ->[\text{Lactate dehydrogenase}] \underbrace{CH3-\!\!\!\!\!{\overset{\overset{\Huge\;\,{\ce{OH}}}|}{\enspace\;{\ce{CH}}}}\!-\!\!{\overset{\overset{\Huge\enspace\!{\ce{O}}}|\!\!|\enspace}{\ce{C}}}\!\!-O^{-}}_{Lactate} + NAD^{+}}\)

Overall, glycolysis of glucose under anaerobic conditions is the following reaction.

\(\ce{\underbrace{C6H12O6}_{Glucose} + 2ADP + 2Pi -> 2\underbrace{CH3-\!\!\!\!\!{\overset{\overset{\Huge\;\,{\ce{OH}}}|}{\enspace\;{\ce{CH}}}}\!-\!\!{\overset{\overset{\Huge\enspace\!{\ce{O}}}|\!\!|\enspace}{\ce{C}}}\!\!-O^{-}}_{Lactate} + 2ATP}\)

The two \(\ce{NADH}\) produced in the glycolysis of one glucose are consumed in the anaerobic conversion of two pyruvates into two lactates.

  • There is a net gain of two energetic molecules, i.e., \(\ce{2ATP}\) in glycolysis of one glucose followed by anaerobic conversion of two pyruvates into two lactates.
  • During hard exercise, lactate and H+ build up in the muscle. The H+, not the lactate, contributes to the burning feeling and fatigue; lactate itself is a fuel, not a poison (Section 13.4). The soreness felt a day or two later comes from small injuries to the muscle fibers, not from lactate. The person keeps breathing heavily after the exercise to pay the oxygen debt. Most of the lactate is transported to the liver, where it is re-oxidized to pyruvate.
Fermentation

Instead of converting pyruvate to lactate, as in humans and animals, yeast has an enzyme called pyruvate decarboxylase that decarboxylates pyruvate to acetaldehyde. Then \(\ce{NADH}\) is oxidized to \(\ce{NAD^{+}}\) at the expense of the reduction of acetaldehyde to ethanol in a process called fermentation, as shown in the reaction below.

Fermentation in yeast: pyruvate loses CO2 to give acetaldehyde, then NADH reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol and regenerates NAD+. (Diagrams: Daniel Kwasniewski, CC BY 4.0.)

The overall reaction of glycolysis of glucose in the fermentation process by yeast.

\(\ce{\underbrace{C6H12O6}_{Glucose} + 2ADP + 2Pi -> 2\underbrace{CH3-CH2-OH}_{Ethanol} + 2CO2 + 2ATP}\)

597203.old:
Insulin -the blood glucose-regulating hormone

Insulin is a hormone that regulates blood glucose levels. The glucose level increases after a meal, and the insulin promotes its absorption into the liver, fat, and muscle cells, converting it into glycogen or fats. High levels of insulin also inhibit the production of glucose by the liver. Low insulin levels have the opposite effects, which happen when a person has diabetes.

597203.old:
Two \(\ce{ATP's}\) are produced before the citric acid cycle along with four \(\ce{NADH}\). The citric acid cycle yields \(\ce{GTP's}\), six \(\ce{NADH's}\), and two \(\ce{FADH2{'s}}\). \(\ce{GTP's}\) convert to \(\ce{ATP's}\), i.e., one \(\ce{GTP}\) is equivalent to one \(\ce{ATP}\). \(\ce{NADH's}\) and \(\ce{FADH2{'s}}\) enter the electron transport chain and produce heat and \(\ce{ATP's}\). Recall that \(\ce{NADH}\) is more energetic and pumps more protons through complex I, III, and IV than \(\ce{FADH2}\) which is less energetic and pumps fewer protons through complex III and IV only. Therefore, \(\ce{NADH}\) yields more \(\ce{ATP's}\) than \(\ce{FADH2}\). Earlier books state that one \(\ce{NADH's}\) is equivalent to three \(\ce{ATP's}\), but currently accepted average values are the following.

\(\ce{GTP}~ \approx~ 1\ce{ATP}\)

\(\ce{NADH} ~\approx~ 2.5\ce{ATP}\)

\(\ce{FADH2} ~\approx~ 1.5\ce{ATP}\)

Based on these conversions, complete aerobic respiration of glucose produces approximately \(\ce{32ATP's}\), as shown in the following equation and detailed in Table 1.

\(\ce{\underbrace{C6H12O6}_{Glucose} + 6O2 + 10NAD^{+} + 2FAD + 2GDP + 2ADP + 4Pi -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + 10NADH + 2FADH2 + 2GTP + 2ATP}\)

\(\ce{\underbrace{C6H12O6}_{Glucose} + 6O2 +32ADP + 32Pi -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + 32ATP}\)

The melting point and boiling point for methylamine are predicted to be significantly greater than those of ethane. CH3CH3 and CH3NH2 are similar in size and mass, but methylamine possesses an −NH group and therefore may exhibit hydrogen bonding.
